title: Shloka 161
subtitle: Outside cause and effect, and therefore at play

namas.translation: Nothing produced her and she follows from nothing, so the chain of dependence that binds other things has no grip on her.

children.gloss: effect, what is to be brought about
cause, that from which something proceeds

namas.translation: Amorous play moves through her as waves move through water, each crest lifting the next.
Gold catches the light at her ears, and the flash of those ornaments is often the first thing a worshipper sees of her face.

compound.gloss: whose earrings are of glittering gold

namas.translation: The form she takes is put on for sport, worn the way a player wears a costume and set down again as easily.

compound.gloss: she who wears a body assumed for play

children.gloss: a body taken on for sport
play, sport, mere semblance assumed in play
she who bears, wears or holds

commentary.meaning: Four names, and the first and last of them are an argument. She is released from cause and effect: nothing made her, and nothing follows from her by the kind of necessity that makes one thing follow from another. She wears a body for play: since no necessity operates on her, whatever she does can only be sport. Between the premise and the conclusion the verse puts two entirely concrete things — amorous play running through her in waves, and gold catching the light at her ears. That placement is the point. A reader who has just been told that she stands outside the causal order might expect the next names to withdraw further into abstraction. Instead the hymn gives her a body, an ornament and a mood, and then explains the body as a costume. The description is not a concession to weaker minds; it is what the first name licenses. Only something uncaused can afford to be decorative.
commentary.history:
Kārya and kāraṇa are the working vocabulary of Indian philosophy rather than poetic diction, and the compound is doing technical work. Kārya is a gerundive of √kṛ — that which is to be made, hence the product; kāraṇa is the agent-instrument noun from the same root, that from which the product proceeds. The Sāṃkhya analysis that stands behind most later Hindu cosmology sorts the whole of reality by exactly this pair: root nature is cause and never effect, the intellect and the ego and the subtle elements are both cause and effect, the last sixteen principles are effect only, and the conscious self is neither. To call her nirmuktā of both is to place her where that scheme places consciousness, at the one position in the table that the chain of production does not touch. The interest of the name is that the hymn has elsewhere identified her with root nature as well, and so refuses to let the two positions stay apart.

The consequence is the doctrine of līlā, and the classical formulation of it is a single line of the Brahmasūtra which answers an objection. If the absolute is complete, it can want nothing; if it wants nothing, it has no motive to produce a world; and an act without motive is unintelligible. The reply is that the act is like play in ordinary life, which people undertake without any purpose outside itself. Śaṅkara's comment adds the familiar examples — breathing, which happens without deliberation, and the games of a king who already has everything. Play is not a lesser mode of action here. It is the only mode of action available to something that lacks nothing, and it is therefore the technical term for divine activity as such.

Taraṅgita, the participle in the second name, is built on taraṅga, a wave, itself from √tṛ, to cross over. The image of an unmoved ocean rippling into waves is one of the standard Vedāntic figures for how a changeless reality can present change, and it is a favourite of Śākta poetry in particular: the most famous hymn to this goddess is called a laharī, a flood or wave, of beauty. What the name adds is what is rippling. Kāmakeli is amorous play, keli being the ordinary word for dalliance and sport, and the compound therefore says that the erotic is not an episode in her life but the medium in which her whole surface moves. Śrīvidyā takes the union of Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī as its central image of reality, and the hymn returns to that pair repeatedly; this name reports the same union as motion rather than as tableau.

A tāṭaṅka is not a small earring. It is the large disc or plug that distends the lobe, the ornament familiar from South Indian bronzes, and in ordinary usage it is the emblem of the married woman whose husband is alive. Around the great goddess temples of the Tamil country there grew up a body of tradition making that emblem cosmically load-bearing — the earrings are said to hold Śiva's own auspiciousness in place, and the periodic renewal of the tāṭaṅkas of Akhilāṇḍeśvarī at Tiruvanaikkaval, popularly credited to Śaṅkara, is performed as an act of consequence for the world and not only for the shrine. These are late and local traditions rather than anything the hymn states, but they show what kind of object the name is pointing to.

Kanat is a present participle of √kan, to shine or to be pleased, and it is rare enough to feel deliberately archaic. Placed against kanaka, gold, which the traditional etymologists derive from the same root, it produces a jingle that is also a small argument: the gold is glittering because glittering is what gold is. Vigraha, finally, in the last name, is the ordinary word for a body, and specifically for the fashioned body of an image in a shrine. Its literal sense is a taking-apart, from vi plus √grah, which is why the same noun also means a quarrel or a war. A form is a division made in what has no divisions, and the hymn calls the division a game.
commentary.practice:
This verse is one of the places where the hymn organises itself by initial sound, and three of the four names begin with the same syllable. Kāryakāraṇa, kāmakeli, kanatkanaka: three compounds in a row whose first two elements both start with k, and a reciter going at speed can easily produce one of them twice and drop another. Fix them by their subject rather than by their sound — causation, then love, then gold, then the body — and the order will hold.

Two retroflex ṇ's in the verse are there by rule rather than by accident, and hearing why makes them easier to remember. In kāraṇa and in dhāriṇī, a preceding r has pulled the dental n back to the roof of the mouth. This is the ṇatva rule, and once you notice it operating you will start predicting these retroflexes elsewhere in the hymn instead of learning them one at a time. The n of nirmuktā, which has no r before it, stays dental.

The nasal in taraṅgita is ṅ, the velar nasal, and it is followed by g. English speakers reach for the sound in "singer" and stop there; what is wanted is the sound in "finger", nasal and stop both fully present. The same cluster returns in tāṭaṅkā, where it is ṅ followed by k. That word also gives two retroflex stops, ṭ and ṭ, made with the tongue curled back and touching well behind the teeth, and they must not be allowed to soften into the dental t of the neighbouring tara-.

Length discipline matters most in the first name, which has three long ā's in eight syllables — kār, kā, and the final -tā — separated by short vowels that should stay genuinely short. If the shorts creep towards the longs the anuṣṭubh loses its shape immediately. The caesura falls after the sixteenth syllable, at the end of kāmakelitaraṅgitā, and that is the one place to breathe.

For archanā, this verse is a good exercise in the two dative endings, because it contains both. The three ā-stems take -āyai: kāryakāraṇanirmuktāyai namaḥ, kāmakelitaraṅgitāyai namaḥ, kanatkanakatāṭaṅkāyai namaḥ. The fourth name is an ī-stem, and the long ī shortens to the glide y before the ending, giving līlāvigrahadhāriṇyai namaḥ. Getting -iṇyai rather than -iṇīyai right here will serve you for the many agent nouns in -inī that the hymn still has ahead.

As for what the verse asks of the person saying it: it asks you to hold two things together that most religious language keeps apart. You are addressing something that no cause produced, and you are addressing it by way of its jewellery. The verse does not resolve that tension so much as insist that there is none, and the recitation is easier if you stop trying to decide which of the four names is the literal one.

crossReferences.translation: But as in the world, it is mere play.
crossReferences.relevance: The classical answer to the objection that a complete being can have no reason to act, and therefore the doctrinal ground of līlāvigrahadhāriṇī. The sūtra concedes that no motive can be found and turns that into the explanation: what has nothing to gain does not act for gain, it plays. Read alongside kāryakāraṇanirmuktā, the two names of this verse reproduce the objection and the reply in that order.

crossReferences.deva: न च मां तानि कर्माणि निबध्नन्ति धनञ्जय । उदासीनवदासीनमसक्तं तेषु कर्मसु ॥
crossReferences.iast: na ca māṃ tāni karmāṇi nibadhnanti dhanañjaya | udāsīnavad āsīnam asaktaṃ teṣu karmasu ||
crossReferences.translation: And those actions do not bind me, Dhanañjaya, seated as I am like one indifferent, unattached to those actions.
crossReferences.relevance: The same freedom stated from the side of the actor rather than of the metaphysics. Kṛṣṇa has just described himself emitting and reabsorbing the whole order of beings, and then denies that any of it fastens on him. Nirmuktā and nibadhnanti are the two halves of one image, binding and being loosed, and the Gītā's udāsīnavat — like one sitting apart — is as close as the older text comes to calling that activity play.

references.title: Classical Sāṃkhya: An Interpretation of its History and Meaning
references.author: Gerald James Larson (Motilal Banarsidass, 2nd ed. 1979)
references.note: Includes the Sāṃkhyakārikā with translation, and the third kārikā is the table that kāryakāraṇanirmuktā is written against — what is cause only, what is both, what is effect only, what is neither. Fifteen minutes with that verse will do more for this name than any amount of commentary on the hymn itself.

references.title: The Secret of the Three Cities: An Introduction to Hindu Śākta Tantrism
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (University of Chicago Press, 1990)
references.note: The standard scholarly introduction to Śrīvidyā in English, and the place to understand why the erotic register of kāmakelitaraṅgitā is structural rather than ornamental in this tradition. Brooks is careful about what the sources actually say and does not romanticise them.

references.note: Worth opening at √kan for this verse. The entry shows the same root behind kanat, kanaka and a cluster of words for shining and delighting, which is what makes kanatkanaka a small etymological joke rather than a padded compound.
